forms.da: jeg går i biografen af og til
forms.en: I go to the cinema now and then

af og til.explanation: "Af og til" means "now and then" or "from time to time". It is a set phrase of three words, and it sits between "sjældent" (rarely) and "ofte" (often). Example: "Jeg cykler af og til" (I cycle now and then).

sentence.da: Jeg ser min familie **af og til**.
sentence.en: I see my family now and then.

aflyst.explanation: "Aflyst" means "cancelled", for example a train, a flight or an event that will not take place. You will see it on departure boards at stations and airports. It is different from "forsinket" (delayed): a delayed train still comes, a cancelled one does not.

sentence.en: My flight is cancelled.

afrika.explanation: "Afrika" means "Africa". Note the spelling with a K, not a C. Related words are "afrikansk" (African) and "en afrikaner" (an African person).

sentence.da: Han rejser til **Afrika** i næste måned.
sentence.en: He is travelling to Africa next month.

afsted.explanation: "Afsted" means "off" or "away", and it is used about leaving for somewhere: "Vi skal afsted" (We have to get going). It is also written as two words, "af sted". Danes often say "tage afsted" (to head off).

sentence.en: We have to go now.

aftensmad.explanation: "Aftensmad" means "dinner", the main meal of the day, eaten in the evening. It is built from "aften" (evening) and "mad" (food).

sentence.en: What are we having for dinner?

aldrig.explanation: "Aldrig" means "never". It already makes the sentence negative, so you do not add "ikke" (not): "Jeg drikker aldrig kaffe" (I never drink coffee). The opposite is "altid" (always).

sentence.en: I never eat meat.

alene.explanation: "Alene" means "alone" or "on your own". It only says that you are without other people, not that you feel sad. For the feeling of being lonely, say "ensom" (lonely). "Helt alene" means "all alone".

sentence.da: Jeg bor **alene** i en lille lejlighed.
sentence.en: I live alone in a small apartment.

alkohol.explanation: "Alkohol" means "alcohol". You usually say it without "en" in front: "Jeg drikker ikke alkohol" (I do not drink alcohol). On drink menus you will see "alkoholfri" (alcohol-free).

sentence.da: Er der **alkohol** i den her drink?
sentence.en: Is there alcohol in this drink?

alle.explanation: "Alle" means "everyone" or "all": "Alle kan komme" (Everyone can come). "Alle sammen" means "all together" or "all of you". For "everything" use "alt", and for "each" or "every" use "hver".

sentence.en: Everyone in the class can swim.

allerede.explanation: "Allerede" means "already". It often shows that something happened sooner than expected: "Han er allerede her" (He is already here). The opposite idea is "endnu ikke" (not yet).

sentence.en: You are here already!

allergisk.explanation: "Allergisk" means "allergic". To say what you are allergic to, Danish uses "over for" where English says "to": "Jeg er allergisk over for nødder" (I am allergic to nuts).

sentence.en: I am allergic to nuts.

alt.explanation: "Alt" means "everything" or "all": "Alt er godt" (Everything is good). "Alt for" means "far too", as in "alt for dyrt" (far too expensive). For people, use "alle" (everyone) instead.

sentence.en: She has forgotten everything.

altid.explanation: "Altid" means "always", and it is written as one word: "Jeg er altid træt" (I am always tired). The opposite is "aldrig" (never), and "ofte" (often) is the milder word.

sentence.en: He always comes too late.

altså.explanation: "Altså" means "so" or "that means", and Danes also use it for emphasis and a bit like "well" in speech: "Det er altså for dyrt!" (It is really too expensive!). Its exact meaning depends on the situation.

sentence.en: So you are not coming after all?

amerikansk.explanation: "Amerikansk" means "American", used for things from the USA. Unlike in English, it is written with a small letter. A person from the USA is "en amerikaner" (an American).

sentence.en: It is an American film.

anden.explanation: "Anden" means "second" and also "other", so the situation tells you which one is meant: "den anden dør" can be "the second door" or "the other door". For dates, "den anden juni" is the second of June. For more than one thing, use "andre" (others).

sentence.da: Det er den **anden** dør til højre.
sentence.en: It is the second door on the right.

appelsinjuice.explanation: "En appelsinjuice" means "an orange juice". It is built from "appelsin" (orange) and "juice" (juice), and written as one word. In a cafe you can ask for "et glas appelsinjuice" (a glass of orange juice).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have et glas **appelsinjuice**.
sentence.en: I would like a glass of orange juice.

april.explanation: "April" means "April". Unlike in English, month names are written with a small letter in Danish. "Aprilsnar" means "April fool", and it is what Danes call out on 1 April.

sentence.en: The weather is changeable in April.

arabisk.explanation: "Arabisk" means "Arabic", and it is used for the language and for things from the Arab world. Unlike in English, it is written with a small letter: "Hun taler arabisk" (She speaks Arabic).

sentence.en: She speaks both Danish and Arabic.

asien.explanation: "Asien" means "Asia". Note the ending: "Asien", not "Asia". Related words are "asiatisk" (Asian) and "en asiat" (an Asian person).

sentence.en: We are going on holiday in Asia.

at arbejde.explanation: "At arbejde" means "to work": "Jeg arbejder på et hospital" (I work at a hospital). "Et arbejde" also means "a job" or "work" itself: "Jeg har meget arbejde" (I have a lot of work). The spelling with -ejd- does not look like it sounds, so watch it.

sentence.en: I work in an office.

atten.explanation: "Atten" means "eighteen". Be careful with the spelling: it is "atten", not "otteten", even though 8 is "otte".

sentence.da: Hun er **atten** år og bor hjemme.
sentence.en: She is eighteen and lives at home.

august.explanation: "August" means "August". Unlike in English, Danish month names are written with a small letter, so it is "august".

sentence.en: School starts again in August.

australien.explanation: "Australien" means "Australia". A person from there is "en australier" (an Australian person), and "australsk" means "Australian" when you describe something, as in "australsk vin" (Australian wine).

sentence.en: My brother lives in Australia.

en adresse.explanation: "En adresse" means "an address", the place where someone lives or gets post. A Danish address puts the street name first and then the number, as in "Vestergade 12". The postcode comes before the town, as in "8000 Aarhus".

sentence.en: What is your address?

en afgang.explanation: "En afgang" means "a departure", for example of a train, bus or plane. You will see it on timetable boards next to "ankomst" (arrival). For a person going away, Danes more often say "at tage afsted" (to set off).

sentence.en: The departure is at nine o'clock.

en aftale.explanation: "En aftale" means "an appointment" or "an agreement". "At have en aftale" (to have an appointment) is used for plans, for example at the doctor's. People also say "Det er en aftale!" for "It's a deal!".

sentence.en: I have an appointment with the doctor.

en aften.explanation: "En aften" means "an evening". Useful phrases are "i aften" (tonight), "om aftenen" (in the evening, as a habit) and "god aften" (good evening). The word is also part of "aftensmad" (the evening meal).

sentence.en: We are eating together tonight.

en agurk.explanation: "En agurk" means "a cucumber". Do not mix it up with "en salat", which means lettuce or a whole salad.

sentence.en: I am cutting a cucumber for the salad.

en albue.explanation: "En albue" means "an elbow". Danish says "the elbow" where English says "my elbow": "Jeg har slået albuen" is literally "I have hit the elbow", meaning "I have hit my elbow".

sentence.en: I hit my elbow on the table.

en alder.explanation: "En alder" means "an age", how old someone is. To ask someone's age, Danes say "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?) rather than using "alder", which sounds more formal, like on a form. You will also see it in "i min alder" (at my age).

sentence.en: What is your age?

en allergi.explanation: "En allergi" means "an allergy". In a restaurant you can say "Jeg har en allergi" (I have an allergy) or be specific, as in "Jeg har en nøddeallergi" (I have a nut allergy). The end is said like "-ee".

sentence.da: Jeg har en **allergi** over for nødder.
sentence.en: I have an allergy to nuts.

en ambulance.explanation: "En ambulance" means "an ambulance", and it looks much like the English word. In an emergency you can say "Jeg har brug for en ambulance" (I need an ambulance).

sentence.en: Call for an ambulance!

en amerikaner.explanation: "En amerikaner" means "an American", a person from the USA, and it is used for both men and women. Unlike in English, the Danish word does not start with a capital letter. The word that describes something as American is "amerikansk".

sentence.da: Hun er **amerikaner**, men bor i Danmark.
sentence.en: She is American but lives in Denmark.

en ananas.explanation: "En ananas" means "a pineapple". It looks nothing like the English word, but "ananas" is used in many other languages, so you may already know it.

sentence.en: I love fresh pineapple.

en and.explanation: "En and" means "a duck". Be careful: "anden" (the duck) is spelled like "anden" meaning "other" or "second", as in "den anden" (the other one), so the context shows which is meant.

sentence.en: The children are feeding the duck by the lake.

en ankomst.explanation: "En ankomst" means "an arrival". On boards in stations and airports it sits opposite "afgang" (departure). The matching verb is "at ankomme" (to arrive).

sentence.en: The arrival is at twelve o'clock.

en app.explanation: "En app" means "an app", a small program on your phone or tablet, the same word as in English. To download one Danes say "at hente en app" (literally "to fetch an app"), and to open it "at åbne appen".

sentence.en: I use the app every day.

en appelsin.explanation: "En appelsin" means "an orange", the fruit. English uses "orange" for both the fruit and the colour, but Danish has two words: "appelsin" for the fruit and "orange" for the colour. Orange juice is "appelsinjuice".

sentence.en: I peeled an orange for the children.

en arm.explanation: "En arm" means "an arm". Danish often says "the arm" where English says "her arm": "Hun har brækket armen" is literally "She has broken the arm", meaning "She has broken her arm".

sentence.en: He has broken his arm.

en avis.explanation: "En avis" means "a newspaper". You say "at læse avisen" (to read the paper). For news online, "nyheder" (news) is a handy word too.

sentence.en: My dad reads the newspaper every morning.

et ansigt.explanation: "Et ansigt" means "a face". Useful examples are "Vask dit ansigt" (Wash your face) and "et glad ansigt" (a happy face).

sentence.en: She has a beautiful face.

et apotek.explanation: "Et apotek" means "a pharmacy", the shop where you buy medicine. The person working there is "en farmaceut" (a pharmacist). Say "på apoteket" for "at the pharmacy".

sentence.da: Jeg skal på **apoteket** og købe medicin.
sentence.en: I need to go to the pharmacy and buy medicine.

et arbejde.explanation: "Et arbejde" means "a job" or "work". Danes say "på arbejde" (at work): "Jeg er på arbejde" means "I am at work", and "at gå på arbejde" means "to go to work". The action is "at arbejde" (to work).

sentence.en: I have to go to work now.
